gi26lh.title: Nintendo on how it sets hardware and software prices
gi26lh.content: Nintendo has shared a ton of different comments about its approach to pricing for hardware and software. This comes from president Shuntaro Furukawa as well as the company’s Ko Shiota, Shinya Takahashi, and Yusuke Beppu.We’ll focus on Furukawa’s comments. Speaking during an investor Q&A this week, he said that for hardware, it’s about “components supplied by numerous partners, making production costs sensitive to external conditions.” Nintendo will look to absorb moderate cost increases, but price increases happen “if we determine that the impact is too significant to be managed through our own efforts over the medium to long term, and that maintaining a healthy profit structure has become difficult.”Regarding software prices, Furukawa mentioned that physical games are impacted by rising component costs, though not as much as hardware. That said, Nintendo looks to set prices here “that reflect the value of each individual title” and “based on its specific content.”You can find the full comments from Furukawa, Shiota, Takahashi, and Beppu below.Furukawa: Our approach to pricing differs between hardware and software. Hardware manufacturing relies on components supplied by numerous partners, making production costs sensitive to external conditions. Currently, various external factors are driving up manufacturing costs. Our fundamental policy is to maintain retail prices as much as possible: for moderate cost increases, we strive to absorb them through internal efforts – such as improving production efficiency – or by covering the additional costs ourselves. However, if we determine that the impact is too significant to be managed through our own efforts over the medium to long term, and that maintaining a healthy profit structure has become difficult, we must then consider price adjustments.As for software, while the impact on physical (packaged) games – which use memory chips in their game cards – is more limited than it is for hardware, they are still affected by rising component costs, so the situation is not necessarily ideal. That said, our core policy for software is to set prices that reflect the value of each individual title. Rather than applying a uniform pricing structure, we evaluate and determine the price for each piece of software based on its specific content.Shiota: In Nintendo’s approach to product creation, our primary focus is not on adopting the latest or most advanced technology for its own sake, but rather on the entertainment experience we deliver to our customers. We invest in the elements necessary to realize that experience, while in other areas, we may choose to limit features or scale back performance. This type of decision-making is a key principle in how Nintendo designs its hardware. Furthermore, when considering hardware specifications, it is crucial to also examine how software can function in an engaging way on that hardware. Therefore, our hardware and software developers work closely together, discussing and determining these specifications as a unified team. This has long been a fundamental principle of Nintendo’s approach to product creation – a philosophy we intend to carry forward.Takahashi: In software development, our priority is to create unique products that offer customers value exceeding their price. We believe that when many customers choose these products and enjoy them over a long period, it ultimately leads to stable earnings. From the perspective of software development, our role is to consider how we can leverage the unique features of our hardware to propose new forms of play and entertainment.Beppu: Nintendo’s fundamental approach to pricing involves assessing the inherent value of a product or service and then incorporating various added values ​​and services. In the long term, our goal is to enhance the value of our offerings and set prices that reflect that value, thereby encouraging more customers to choose our products.As the range of entertainment options continues to expand, customers are becoming increasingly selective in what they choose. Consequently, for customers to select our offerings, it is essential that we firmly position products with a distinct, “Nintendo-esque” character within our lineup.For the past 40 years or so, our software business has centered on packaged software. Moving forward, to further elevate the value of each of our IPs, it will be important to go beyond simply releasing individual titles; we must consistently provide products and services that inspire customers to keep engaging with our content. … The ability to play with others serves as a compelling reason for people to choose our products, and this, in turn, helps expand the circle of players. While this may also indirectly influence our pricing, we believe that creating the motivation and opportunities for people to play together is essential to enhancing the value that Nintendo offers.

191zyxo.title: Nintendo not giving up on pursuing new forms of play, says offering unique entertainment “is our company’s lifeblood”
191zyxo.content: During a financial results Q&A, Nintendo was asked if the priority placed on developing new forms of play has declined. While we haven’t seen something revolutionary like the Wii as of late, that doesn’t mean it’s not a focus.Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa responded to the question by saying that there’s been “absolutely no decline in the management priority we place on creating new forms of play through the integrated development of hardware and software.” He would add that offering unique entertainment “is our company’s lifeblood.”Furukawa as well as Nintendo’s Shinya Takahashi and Ko Shiota shared the following: Furukawa: There has been absolutely no decline in the management priority we place on creating new forms of play through the integrated development of hardware and software. Providing unique entertainment—the kind only Nintendo can offer—is our company’s lifeblood. Over the past 40 years or so, it is precisely this integrated approach that has enabled us to deliver such experiences. While it is possible that in the future we might offer unique entertainment in a different form, we believe that, at present, the integrated development of hardware and software is the best way to fully leverage our strengths. We will continue to prioritize the creation of unique entertainment that is distinctly Nintendo.Takahashi: Our hardware and software development teams work as one to create entirely new forms of play that take full advantage of the capabilities and features of new hardware. In this process, our fundamental approach is not to start by focusing on the new features themselves, but rather to first conceive an engaging gameplay experience, then determine what new hardware features are required to bring that experience to life, and finally, maximize the utility of those features. We are currently engaged in a process of trial and error to realize new forms of play for the successor to the Nintendo Switch, so please look forward to the day we can share more details.Shiota: The practice of hardware and software developers working together—sharing ideas and engaging in repeated trial and error to create new forms of entertainment—is a development culture that has long defined Nintendo. Having been involved in development for a long time since joining the company, I can say that while the technologies we use and the forms our products take may evolve, this core mindset among our developers remains unchanged. While only a handful of ideas ultimately evolve into commercial products after much trial and error, we believe it is vital for our management team to invest in the pursuit of concepts that can lead to new forms of enjoyment. Together, we remain fully committed to supporting these efforts. Please look forward to the emergence of unique, new entertainment from us in the future.For more from Furukawa, you can read about what he said regarding the early start for the Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console as well as Ocarina of Time.

1jupeid.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam
1jupeid.content: Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam.Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.”Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data centers until 2030, after a temporary stop that was announced at the end of 2023. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place. The site, being built by British developer Pure Data Centres, has also managed to navigate some loopholes to reach the construction stage.The protests over Microsoft’s data center site in Amsterdam comes in the same week that activists staged a mock Israeli military checkpoint outside a Microsoft data center in Dublin on Tuesday, part of a wave of data center protests across Europe. Earlier this week, voters across the US also rejected unrestrained development of data centers. AI data centers are continuing to pop up across the US, with frequent opposition from locals concerned about the impact on their communities.Microsoft also abandoned the UK’s largest data center project last month, after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s. The software maker has also faced a wave of protests from former employees over the past year. Microsoft’s 50th anniversary party was interrupted by employees protesting the use of Microsoft’s technologies in Israel’s war against Hamas, with one calling Microsoft’s AI CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, a “war profiteer.“A Microsoft employee also disrupted the company’s Build developer conference last year, interrupting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s keynote. Months later, Microsoft fired two employee protesters who occupied its president’s office.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Tom Warren

1k14uv7.title: Sony's Killing This Ratchet & Clank Game Before It Even Comes Out
1k14uv7.content:
Image: Push SquareOne of PlayStation's mobile games is shutting up shop, and it's doing so before it's managed to launch globally.
You may recall Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble, a mobile multiplayer game set within Insomniac Games' beloved sci-fi universe.
It's been quietly making progress with soft launches in specific countries, and was gearing up for a proper, global launch sometime soon. However, developer Oh BiBi has today announced its plans to cease development and close the whole thing down.
The official website for the game has been updated with a notice of the shutdown.
"We've made the difficult decision to cease development of Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble," the statement reads. "The final planned update will be rolling out November 6th, 2026, and the app will be removed from stores on November 21st, 2026."
Players who already have the game can carry on playing through to 1st May 2027, which is the date when the game's servers will permanently go offline. After this point, the game will no longer be playable.
In-app purchases have been removed, and content that was once premium is now available for free, or can be earned through normal play.

The game did release in some countries, including the UK and Canada, as part of a soft launch period before a planned worldwide launch. Back in July, people were invited to pre-register in preparation for the full release, but that will now sadly not be happening.
Ranger Rumble is a competitive multiplayer arena shooter of sorts with cartoonish visuals, various modes to play, and live service elements like time-limited events and seasonal rewards.
On the App Store, the game has a user score of 4.2 (out of 5) after 93 ratings, while it has a 4.4 score after more than 2,000 ratings on Google Play Store.
It's a shame to see the game go down the pan before it really got a proper chance.
Sony does have one or two other mobile games in the pipeline, including Horizon Steel Frontiers, in development at NCSOFT. Hopefully it fares better.
Have you been able to check out Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble? Tell us in the comments section below.

1vxnr8c.title: "It's a brave new world": GTA 6's PC port will release sooner than you think to avoid losing money to AI rip-offs, says former Rockstar tech director
1vxnr8c.content:
"If it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."

Image credit: Take-Two Interactive

GTA 6's PC release may come sooner than anticipated, according to former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, because Rockstar and publishers Take-Two will be concerned about losing money to unofficial generative AI clones of the PS5 version, once it launches on 19th November. In general, Vermeij thinks that how to avoid having your games duplicated by chatbot herders is "the big question" right now for devs and publishers, particularly those who don't have the means to enforce their intellectual property dominions as vehemently as Take-Two do for Grand Theft Auto.
Speaking to me during a wide-ranging chatathon, Vermeij reflected on the early days of Grand Theft Auto development at Rockstar North in the 90s, and how the Noel-and-Liam-Gallagher-esque relationship between PC and console gaming has evolved. He shared a sweary anecdote about the company's difficulties getting the original GTA 1 to look the business on Sony's PlayStation.
"I didn't work on GTA 1 and 2, but I worked for the company at the time, and I was actually right next to the GTA 1 team, so I was able to follow it," he said. "So they worked on PC and then an external company in Dundee did the PlayStation version. Which was really weird, because like, PCs were so much more powerful - still the case, but in those days, it was even more so.
"And I remember, at the time, the GTA team was definitely the most rowdy of all of the teams," Vermeij continued. "And there was one particular day where they sent the PC build away, and then it came back from the PlayStation people, and they had cut down all the textures from 256 colours to 16 colours, and my god, the artist was just going around and swearing - 'what the fuck did they do to our textures, I can't believe it, we can't release this shite'. So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console. So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn't really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better."When it came time to develop GTA 3, Rockstar "flipped that around", Vermeij went on, creating the console versions first. "Clearly the PC market has sort of grown, caught up with the console market, but there's still that same mindset," he said. Most publishers prefer to release all versions at once, Vermeij added, "because then there's only one marketing campaign they have to pay for." GTA lives by its own rules, however. "I guess it's less of an argument for them because the game is just so big, so they just kind of always left it that way. And for developers, it's way easier to just do one version at a time. So, you know, that makes sense."
The arrival of generative AI threatens to throw all this to the winds. Tools such as Reverse Engineer Anything allow for speedy unofficial ports or "slopcomps" of console games on PC, despite warnings from seasoned recomp developers that using genAI for this purpose wrecks the community aspect of unofficial porting, and results in illegible "bruteforce" code rather than preserving some understanding of how the original game was made.
"It really has changed the world," Vermeij observed, "and I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be won't be as good as their effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. So, I wouldn't be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together. Obviously, I don't really know what they're thinking."
GTA 6 is, according to Rockstar and Take-Two at least, an enormously fiddly production, costing hundreds of millions of dollars over eight years in development. Nonetheless, Vermeij thinks current genAI tools are "probably" capable of pulling off a port. "It will take a long time. It actually, physically takes hours and hours and hours to do these things. And it will take a bunch of tokens and everything, so it would probably cost like, tens of thousands of dollars in tokens. But like, you know, if it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."There are already signs that genAI PC port goldrushers are ready to pounce on GTA 6. Just today, Ars Technica reported on efforts to yassify the game's PS5 trailer footage by piping it through a stronker PC graphics card and using Nvidia's DLSS 5 to apply extra layers of gloss.
Vermeij himself left Rockstar way back in 2009 and is now an indie developer. His current early access project is Plentiful, a hexagonal god sim with an emphasis on water physics. It uses "AI-assisted machine translation for localization", but not for "gameplay content, art, or audio". Vermeij is, in general, interested in generative AI despite the surging tide of slopcomp ports. Smaller indie developers are, of course, more vulnerable to the financial fallout from having their work unofficially cloned by generative AI, but Vermeij thinks it's an existential worry for megacorps like Take-Two as well.
"I don't really see how you could protect against that, to be honest," he told me in closing. "I don't see it. But a big company like Take-Two, they would be able to get the lawyers on the case, and maybe, like, you said, for a big game, maybe the AI doesn't really do a particularly good job. But yeah, I mean, it's a brave new world. What was the case before, is that there's so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that's completely changed now. So, yeah, we're going to have to see in the next couple of years, how that's going to pan out."
The latest rumour-mongering places GTA 6's PC release sometime in early 2027. In other news, Rockstar staff are soon to formally vote on whether to apply for union recognition. If the organisers carry the day, the resulting union could encompass nearly all the company's UK staff below management level.

1p9on7q.title: AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities
1p9on7q.content:
AWS recently made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), four months after announcing it in gated preview. The pricing page, which the announcement does not mention, shows a model that charges by the finding as well as by the codebase.

Principal solutions architect Esra Kayabali describes a service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches that can be automated or as pull requests in the connected repositories. It builds a context graph from those repositories and the surrounding AWS environment, with an optional collector supplying resource and network context from wherever the code runs.

Swami Sivasubramanian, VP of Agentic AI, and Christopher Rae, who leads AI security go-to-market at AWS, both framed the problem as volume rather than detection. Sivasubramanian wrote that most organizations running large application estates see thousands of findings a day; Rae put it more bluntly, saying scanners find thousands daily and "most becomes noise that doesn't matter in your environment."

The validation step is the answer to that: rather than ranking by severity, Continuum confirms which findings are reachable by running the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaching proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. Findings carry an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path, and the output is an attack path and "a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone."

Pricing has two dimensions: a context fee covers lines of code protected per month, starting at $200 per million and tiering down to $100 above ten billion. An inference fee charges $10 per Continuum inference unit, consumed as findings are worked. AWS’s worked examples show the interaction: one million lines with 100 vulnerabilities at one unit each comes to $1,200, while 100 million lines with 10,000 vulnerabilities at two units each reaches $218,200. Context accounts for $18,200 of that and inference for the remaining $200,000, or roughly $20 per validated finding. The thousands of daily findings both executives describe, and the per-finding fee, measure the same workload from opposite ends.

Responding on LinkedIn, Bernardo Meireles Correa, an engineer working on non-human and agent identity at Avatier, welcomed the ranking and named two things to watch:

A proof in an isolated sandbox says the code is exploitable. It does not say the path to it exists in your environment, and the findings it cannot prove still need somewhere to go, or they quietly become the safe pile.

The product partly answers the first question: the optional collector gathers AWS resource and network configuration to judge reachability, though as additional setup rather than a default. The second goes unaddressed, since AWS documents what happens to findings it can prove and says nothing about the rest.

Where the announcement points is autonomy. For now, "every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships," and the console warns that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed, but AWS plans to let Continuum apply classes of fix on its own once confidence criteria such as test coverage and historical success rate are met.

(Source: AWS News Blog post)

Jorg Huser, a CTO and former AWS principal, replied to Rae by questioning what should unlock that:

The move from approving each merge to approving a class of fixes deserves its own acceptance test. An overloaded review queue can otherwise become the reason to grant more autonomy. I’d want evidence that the fix removes the vulnerability and preserves expected application behavior. What would qualify a fix class for autonomous merging, and what would send it back to human review?

Google's CodeMender ships something close to that evidence. It also proves exploitability by running an exploit and declines to apply patches itself, and it then validates each patch with an LLM-as-a-judge framework that tests for program equivalence, so the fix resolves the root cause "without altering the application's intended behavior." That is the step AWS's console caveat concedes Continuum does not perform.

The product boundary InfoQ reported in July, when AWS serverless hero Yan Cui said "we have the same capabilities, two product names, and no clarity on which one you should use," is still visible in the documentation: the Continuum user guide covers code vulnerabilities itself and sends readers to a separately titled AWS Security Agent User Guide for penetration testing and threat modeling. Only the code vulnerabilities capability reached general availability. Penetration testing remains separately priced at $50 per task-hour, and threat modeling, announced in preview in June, carries no published pricing.

About the Author

1vdqugq.title: Petition to Save Mass Effect Dev BioWare to Be Considered by Canada's Government
1vdqugq.content:
Paragon action
by Robert RamseyYesterday, 12am

A petition to save BioWare is set to be presented before the Canadian government.
The country's law states that any public petition with at least 500 signatures must be added to the House's agenda — and this fan-driven effort has amassed over 2,300 at the time of writing.
It argues that the Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer is "one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally". It's a fair point.
"BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners, and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy," it rather pointedly continues.
Suggested solutions include providing the company with the "necessary" funding to secure its independence, while also, ideally, recovering IPs like Mass Effect and Dragon Age from EA.

The petition concludes that the government should move to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests."
The closing date for signatures is in March next year.
It's obviously a well-meaning petition driven by passionate fans — but as Eurogamer points out, there may not be much that the Canadian government can do, even if it agrees with the intent.
That's because, ultimately, BioWare — shuttered or not — is owned by EA. As are its aforementioned properties. Even if the country could fund some sort of deal, EA would still have to agree to the whole thing.
Still, the fact that this petition will be officially considered is pretty cool. For a long time, BioWare was considered a jewel in Canada's creative output — a bit like how CD Projekt Red has come to be viewed in Poland.
Do you think there's any genuine hope to this? Hop aboard the Normandy in the comments section below.
[source ourcommons.ca, via eurogamer.net]

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. 1g4d0ak.title: Google Cloud API Gateway Introduces Streaming Support for Real-Time and AI-Powered Applications
1g4d0ak.content:
Google has announced the public preview of streaming support for API Gateway, extending its traditional request-response model to support applications requiring real-time communication. According to Google, this is particularly relevant for AI applications that provide streaming model responses, multi-step agent workflows, and interactive sessions.

The new functionality enables streaming endpoints to operate behind API Gateway while retaining existing gateway policies and security controls, thereby addressing a previous limitation:

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place.

API Gateway supports several streaming patterns, including Server-Sent Events (SSE), chunked transfer encoding and HTTP response streaming, WebSockets, and gRPC. Streaming connections can remain open for up to one hour, after which clients must establish a new connection if continued communication is required.

The new release introduces streaming support without requiring changes to existing API specifications or the use of specific APIs, extensions, or annotations. Google emphasizes that all existing API configurations and capabilities continue to work as before, including API key enforcement, JWT validation, service account authentication to backends, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring integration, and path templating and request routing.

Another benefit of the new release is the introduction of predictable gateway hostnames. Previously, gateway hostnames included a generated hash and could only be determined after the gateway had been created. Now, they follow a deterministic format: GATEWAY_ID-PROJECT_NUMBER.REGION.gateway.dev, allowing developers to reference and configure them before creating the resource.

Google highlights the importance of streaming support for AI applications, where model responses are generated progressively rather than delivered as a single, complete response. Using the new functionality, developers will be able to stream model responses in real time, update agent progress during multi-step tasks, support tool-calling protocols and connections to remote MCP servers, and handle interactive AI applications.

API Gateway also supports model routing, providing a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to route requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload.

Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Commenting on Google's announcement, X user emildrops highlights two important limitations. First, "existing gateways can't be switched in place" and, second, "latency measures the whole stream, not time to first byte... so latency graphs will look broken for reasons that aren't bugs". Similarly, LinkedIn user Ehsan Elahi Zaheer points out that:

Monitoring also needs care: gateway request-latency metrics measure stream duration, not time to first byte. A single latency chart can hide very different user experiences.

During the preview period, developers must explicitly enable the new functionality by specifying the --enable-streaming command-line flag when creating a gateway.

v70lvg.title: Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop
v70lvg.content:
She's got it where it counts

Image credit: Fate of the Galaxy

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.
It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Watch on YouTube

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.
It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.
This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

tc4xex.title: "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site
tc4xex.content:
"We drew the line where the real argument is"

Image credit: Rock Paper Shotgun / Bethesda

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.
"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.
"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot.""While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.
Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.
As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".
I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

nudpdg.title: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0
nudpdg.content:
Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette.
These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent. This release improves that integration:

Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing #, which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view.
New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first.
app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created.
The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel.

142qh1l.title: "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games
142qh1l.content:
"We can only assume"

Image credit: Studio Daimon

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

Watch on YouTube

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

khht29.title: Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"
khht29.content:
Speak now

Image credit: Embark

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.
In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?
Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.

pa6u9t.title: Zero Trust Agent Systems that Pass Audits and Still Ship
pa6u9t.content:
Transcript

Advait Patel: Today, I'm going to talk about something that I have been working on for the past couple of months, maybe a year or so. My talk presentation is, "Zero Trust Agent Systems That Pass Audits and Still Ship." I work as a senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, where I work on the large-scale multi-tenant cloud environments. Most of the times my job is about securing those environments in cloud deployments, cloud environments, and making sure that they still ship on time. Apart from that, I have been researching into cloud security and LLM intersection. I have been also part of the cloud CSA alliance group. I'm also project creator for DockSec, which is adopted by OWASP, and also have been founding member for one of the OWASP projects called AIVSS, Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System. Apart from that, I was fortunate to be invited at multiple flagship conferences such as QCon AI. Also, I was invited to speak at SANS CloudSecNext in Denver last year. Also, I will be speaking to OWASP Global AppSec in Austria, Vienna.

How many of you are running AI agents in your production environment? How many of you are still thinking, and are probably in the pilot phase of running AI agents? Today, for folks who are already in production, I'm going to show you what controls you can implement in your production environment for AI agents this week. Also, the folks who are still in planning phase, I'm going to save some time and will share some of the learnings that I saw or some of the things that I made mistakes while implementing these AI agents in production.

One Bad Day with an Agent

Let's start with a bad story. There was a team who faced this in a real environment, in a production environment. They were running an AI agent, and that AI agent was specifically designed for their support system. The job for that agent was very simple. A support ticket comes in, AI agents read it, it goes to the documentation, it fetches the documentation, and then it prepares the steps for the support engineer, and it makes the support engineers' lives easier. Sounds easy. That was all. It was running perfectly fine in the production environment, everyone was happy with it. Some random Tuesday afternoon, that AI agent started making API calls to the production database. That AI agent had literally no business to make those calls. There were no user instructions as well that literally told it to do so. Still, it made the call because it thought that it would help it to answer the question better.

It did. The worst part was, the AI agent made the calls, and whatever result that it got from those tools call, it passed it downstream, and eventually it ended up in the external APIs. That's how the data crossed the tenant boundaries, and it ended up sharing outside the environment. This entire thing was caught in 45 minutes. This was caught because there was no security control. There was no security mechanism that the team built. Because there was an on-call engineer who was looking at the dashboard, and all of a sudden, he saw a huge spike in the logs, and that's how he caught it, so 45 minutes. In those 45 minutes, that agent made the wrong API calls, it went to the production database. It passed those results into the downstream API and made some external email APIs, and then it was breached. How they caught it? Because some engineer got curious, and he saw the unusual spike in the logs. This is not how we do it, this is not the best practice, and still, it happened. This is the talk, is the playbook I wish that I had in that week, or someone or any engineer had that in that week.

Agents Aren't a New Model, They're a New Identity

When people talk about AI agents, they all think about some beautiful, nice, and fancy chatbots that can make their lives easier and all. Today, here, I need you to think about it differently. Today, I need you to think about that AI agents are not a new model, but those are a new identity. These AI agents are running in your environment, they're running in your system. Whatever controls or whatever security mechanism that you guys have built in your system, they are not applicable to this new identity. We need something to fight against this identity, because this is a fundamentally different aspect of your system. If you compare this new identity with other components in your system, they are completely different, because these new identities, they decide autonomously. They decide which API calls they need to make next, doesn't matter if it is your billing API, doesn't matter if it is your production database API, doesn't matter if it is your external email API.

If that agent thinks that it needs to do it to better easily answer the question, it will do so. This is how it is different first. Second is it holds state. Whatever that it ran in step one, it stores that context, it stores that information with it, and it still uses in step seven, doesn't matter if step one and step seven are different, but it still uses it if it thinks that it's helpful. The third is outruns review. By the time your engineer opens a ticket, by the time your engineer files and reports the issue, that agent will act faster, it will act in milliseconds, seconds, and then it will make 40 different API calls, it will call 40 different tools within a fraction of a second. This is before anyone can even recognize the issue or before anyone can even file the issue. That is why these are the new attackers. This is why this is a new identity where we don't have a security mechanism or we don't have any controls in place to handle or to fight against these identities.

Before we go one step further into any technical details, 18 months ago, if you folks were sitting in your audits and in front of your auditor, and if your auditor asked you about AI agents, that was unusual. Now it is a standard. Your auditors need answers from your AI agents. They will ask you about SOC 2 and ISO reviewers. They ask about the agent-specific questions during the evidence collection. HIPAA and PCI scopes are catching those agent data flows that touch regulated fields. Internal risk committees want explainability per action, not per session. Let me ask you one question. Also, I want you folks to remember it as well, that in next year's audit, and you are sitting in front of an auditor, and if the auditor asks you about how you guys control what AI agents can do in your system, and if you answer it like, maybe LLM decides, or our own LLM, whether you are running it external or internal, my own LLM decides it. Then that auditor will write it up, and then you will have a finding. Those answers are not going to work nowadays.

Four Failure Modes I See in Production

Let me ask you about the AI security. When someone talks about AI security, people will refer to it as hallucination. I get it. Hallucinations are real, and that is a real question and real problem. Hallucinations are only limited, or that hallucination problem is up to the model layer, not the tool layer. Today, I need you to think about a different problem, which sits at the tool layer, and not the model layer, because that is where the blast radius lives. These four problems which I have listed here, are real problems that I saw and I faced in real production environments. The first problem is prompt injection via tool output. Up to this point, we were thinking that prompt injection via user input is the problem. For example, your user enters something malicious in your LLM algorithm or maybe chatbot, and then something happens, some bad activity or some malicious activity happens, and that is why you think that this happened because of the bad user query.

No, we are not seeing that in production environments, because we are all coming from a technical background, and we are all engineers. This is not happening in a production environment. What happens is prompt injection happens via tool output. Whatever your tool gives you, doesn't matter if it is a web page, doesn't matter if it is a document, or doesn't matter whatever instructions it is, they are malicious. Those retrieved documents is the real attacker here, because assume that those documents that tool retrieves, those documents that tool receives at the output phase, they can have anything, any malicious thing. We will see in the upcoming demo what it can be. Anything can be written in the document, and that LLM will blindly follow it, and then it will act accordingly, and then you have an outage. You have a data breach. The second is privilege creep. Assume that your agent is now calling 10 different tools, and each tool has its own set of access and permissions, and now nobody in your team sat down and reviewed those permissions.

Nobody in your team sat down and think about whether this agent actually needs this many permissions or not, because all of those tools in combination gave that agent hundreds of permissions and hundreds of access, because no one was there to review it, and now it accumulated by composition. The third thing is unsafe retrieval. Context crosses tenant and sensitivity boundaries at retrieval time, because a query for one particular customer, the output and everything will be with the AI agents, and AI agents can now use that same output for other customers as well. With this situation, one customer data is crossing the boundaries and going to another customer data. This is the third problem, unsafe retrieval. The fourth is action amplification, like one ambiguous prompt that goes into the dozens of other side-effectful calls, because that agent thought that, ok, I will need these calls to make the answer better. These are the four failure modes that we are seeing in this production environment.

Threat Model and Reference Architecture

This is the architecture, this is the slide that I present whenever I talk to an internal team or whenever I talk to a compliance team and all. On your left side, there is a demo threat model. Usually, people think that a user talks to an LLM, and then that is it. These are the only two entities that are in the demo threat model, user and LLM. On your right side, that is the actual production threat model, what we can actually see in production. First of all, user talks to LLM, then LLM talks to tools, and then tools, they talk to the database or your data layer. Then those data pass downstream, those data go downstream. Then they affect the real humans. This is how the actual production threat model works. The blast radius leaves past the LLM, where the agent touches the real system. Every control in this talk lives on the right side of this diagram, where there are multiple entities as well apart from user and LLM, and we will see in the upcoming demo how this affects the entire model. Today, I want you to remember one thing. It doesn't matter if you don't remember anything else, but just remember one thing that the prompt is not the boundary, but the tool layer is actually the actual boundary.

We talked about the problem, we talked about the challenges, and we also talked about what we see and what was the bad actors, bad story, and everything. This is the diagram. This is how I solve it. This is how I overcame the solution, and this is how I fixed it. Before we go into this architecture diagram, take a note of it. I'm going to deep dive individually in all the layers one by one, and this is the architecture diagram that we present in front of auditors as well when we talk about how we are handling AI agents in a production environment. Also, each layer, the order matters, and also each layer assumes that the one layer above is already in place and already in working condition, and we cannot skip the layers as well.

What Each Layer Enforces

Let's go into layers in detail. Let's start with the first layer, which is the identity layer. This is the foundation layer. This is the fundamental layer where everything starts. This is the identity where each agent will get its own identity. Each agent, each separate session will have its own identity. It doesn't matter if it is doing x number of accounts. It doesn't matter if it is doing x number of steps, or it doesn't matter whatever it touches, but every session, every agent will get its own identity. For example, I use Workload Identity at work. If you are using Google, GCP products, then you have Workload Identity. If you are using AWS products, then you have AWS IAM roles, or if you are using multi-tenant Kubernetes environment, then you have SPI/FFP, as in Workload Identity. Every agent, every token, every session will get its own identity. When an auditor will ask these questions like, show me how you tie this action to a specific agent and a specific user, this is the layer that you come and you show the evidence about what sort of agent and what sort of identity that it used. This sits in the first and fundamental layer of the architecture.

The second layer is tools layer. This is very important. This is where most of the teams get it wrong. This is the important layer because your agents are using multiple tools, because in a production environment you cannot have one agent for one tool. It will be expensive. You have one agent using multiple tools, but each tool layer can have its own identity. It can have its own authorization, rate limit, I/O decisions. Doesn't matter what it is controlling, all the input, all the output. Also, it uses the short-lived tokens because we have to restrict the tokens usage as well. Each tool cannot have hours and hours of long operations tokens. If that work is done, then token can also get expired. We don't have to use the same token for other work. That's how we need to control it. When an auditor asks you, show me the token which was used for this call, then this is the layer that you should come and you should show the token. "This was the token that was used for this task. These are the operations that were made. These are the users who actually were attached to that token."

The third layer is context and retrieval layer. This is where you actually enforce the policy, because as a tool gave you the output in your document or web page format, this is where you actually enforce the ACLs per document. If your ACLs are saying, ok, you need to set these instructions and you don't need to skip these instructions, then this is the layer where it will be applicable. Because you cannot control this from the model layer, you cannot control this from the prompt layer, but it has to be here. It has to be in the context and retrieval layer. Basically, you cannot restrict what a user enters. You can have thousands of keywords, but those are not enough, because the LLM doesn't work in your favor when it comes to presenting the output. This is where you need to actually implement the ACLs, and you need to show, ok, these are the policies that I want this model or this agent to follow.

When an auditor asks you, show me the ACLs applied to the document retrieved here, then this is the answer to your question. Then, another important aspect of the architecture is the policy and decision layer. This is where the agent will decide, what I should enforce and what I should just pass on. This is the separate engine that sits between AI agent's intent and execution. This is where the decisions get logged. As an agent, how that agent decided to pass this to the next step or how the agent decided to flag it and not pass it to another state. This is where the policy and all those controls, like for example, people use OPA, people use Cedar, or they have their own custom rules as well. Those custom rules and everything will be applied here. Now if your auditor asks you, show me the policy version that was active during this incident, then this is your answer.

The last and important part of this architecture is audit and evidence. This is where you have the provability, this is where you have the actual evidence. Nowadays, like with AI agents, you cannot capture the screenshots, you cannot capture the email evidence enough. This is where you can actually show the traces, this is where actually you show the observability and prove that whatever the agent did and everything is traceable. This is the step where structured trace per action is needed, and those traces are tied per identity and per session. Now, just assume that an auditor asks you, walk me through that, what happened. Like for example, in the previous scenario that we discussed, an auditor comes and says, now show me what happened, how that happened and at what time. Now you have the traces where you can show, this was the agent, it uses that token, and these are the tools that it called and these are the actions that it performed, and these are the decisions that it flagged, or these are the decisions that it made.

Tradeoffs You'll Hit, At Scale

If I just show you the clean picture, if I show you, these are the things that work in production, these are the things that you need to do in production, I'm not going to help you. Because these are the tradeoffs that I saw in an actual production environment. The first tradeoff was decisions in the hot path, because before you budget your tool, before you budget your AI agents and action, you also need to consider the latency as well, because one agent makes maybe tens or twenties of tools for that work. Each tool can take from 5 milliseconds to 20 milliseconds per call, so you also have to budget that when you sign or when you consider about SLAs. The second is token lifecycle. We talked about one token per work. We talked about one token per session. For example, if that call is lengthier than you expect, then token may or may not get expired within the work, and at that time, your AI agent workflow can be broken.

At that time, you need to think about, either I need to stop the agent, I need to kill the agent, or I need to let it run. This is the token lifecycle that usually is affected if there are lengthier tasks. The third tradeoff is fail-open versus fail-close, and that is where only you and your team can decide what sort of mechanism or thing that you need to put in fail-open versus fail-close. Thumb rule, which I follow, is I always put destructive operations in fail-close and read-only operations in fail-open, because if something bad happens, and if central policy agent gets broken, then I would rather stop my AI agent taking any destructive operations than stopping it from reading the tickets or reading the customer stories. This is where only you can decide what sort of operations that you want to allow in case of failure and what sort of operations that you want to just pass in case of failure.

The fourth point for tradeoff is cardinality, where per-session identity explodes label cardinality in traces and metrics, and this is something that usually surprised me most. The last one is policy as single point of failure. For example, you have one policy engine sits in the middle, sits in the central, and if it gets failed, then all of your AI agents will get messed up. They won't know which policy to implement and which policy to act upon. You need some sort of backup mechanism, where in case of failure of a central policy agent, you also have some backup where those AI agents can go and talk to.

Guardrails

Guardrails and identity and tools. Before we talk about guardrails, why do we need guardrails? Every AI agent needs some boundaries so that they can work within that boundary and also you have some control over it. The first guardrail which is very important is least privilege at the tool layer. What we do is we implement least privilege control at the prompt layer, but that is the wrong start. You cannot control user to enter the prompt. You can control the keywords that they can enter, but that is bad practice because it should happen at the tool
